 Storm brings hazardous road conditions as local agencies prepare across Fresno County 
 Downed trees, rain, gloomy skies, and strong wind gusts were already affecting the San Joaquin Valley as a storm system moved through California, creating slick roads and hazardous driving conditions. KFSN By Brisa Colón Saturday, November 14, 2026 1:17AM Share FRESNO COUNTY, Calif. (KFSN) -- Downed trees, rain, gloomy skies, and strong wind gusts were already affecting the San Joaquin Valley as a storm system moved through California, creating slick roads and hazardous driving conditions.
 "Unfortunately, the weather, we see it all the time, there's going to be an increase not only in traffic crashes but in calls for service, not only for the Highway Patrol but also for local law enforcement and emergency services," said Mike Salas with the California Highway Patrol.
 Salas urged drivers to inspect their tires, windshield wipers and lights before heading out and to allow extra travel time for delays caused by the weather.
 "We're going to be out there in force; you're going to see a lot of the black-and-white patrol cars, mainly just in view. Patrols trying to slow down the public," Salas said.
 The storm was also worsening road conditions across county and city streets, where large potholes were already present.
 Fresno County crews spent the summer preparing for wet weather conditions. This year, crews used new mapping technology and GoPro cameras to document trouble spots.
 "What we get from the National Weather Service is on a daily basis on these storm events, which are shared with our maintenance teams in our road maintenance teams in our 9 road yards," said Steve White, Fresno County public works director.
 County officials have strategically placed more than 200 K-rails throughout the county in case roads need to be closed. Heavy equipment is also on standby.

 "We have dump trucks, semi-trailer trucks, drop-dead trucks, we have loaders, Bacos, snowplows, excavators, Bob Cats, and all the other small hand tools and equipment," White said.
 In the city, residents can report issues through the FresGO app and the 311 service, which track potholes, flooding, and roadway maintenance concerns. The app displays a map of open requests and updates as crews' complete repairs.
 "We have over 18-hundred miles of roads and there's no way we can cover them all without the public's help," said Brian Russell, public works director.
 Officials are encouraging residents to report roadway issues and drive cautiously during the storm.
 The county also has an emergency website up and running, and you can find it here .
